prompt.context: Your client is the UK's National Gallery, a government-funded heritage institution with the mission of welcoming the public to explore and experience art and creativity. Due to decreasing available government funding for the creative sector in recent years, the National Gallery has set a goal to grow profitability from commercial activities.
prompt.question: What factors would you like to review to understand how the National Gallery could improve its profitability?

clarifying_info.q: What does the National Gallery's current income consist of?
clarifying_info.a: Income includes government funding, donations, and revenue from commercial activities.

clarifying_info.q: What types of costs does the National Gallery incur?
clarifying_info.a: Two types: (1) costs incurred as a direct result of running revenue-generating business activities, such as staging a ticketed exhibition or catering in cafes and restaurants; (2) costs incurred while fulfilling its public mission, such as collecting artwork, contributing to art history research, and hosting study tours for school children.

clarifying_info.q: Does the National Gallery charge for entry?
clarifying_info.a: Entry to the National Gallery is free for all, but tickets are sold for special exhibitions.

clarifying_info.q: How many days a week is the National Gallery open?
clarifying_info.a: The National Gallery is open 6 days a week (closed on Mondays).

clarifying_info.q: What are the objectives beyond improving profitability?
clarifying_info.a: Improving profitability while continuing to fulfil its mission of welcoming the public to explore and experience art and creativity.

exhibits.title: Revenue and Costs of Special Exhibitions
exhibits.shows: Lists revenue drivers and cost structure for special exhibitions

revenue: ~500,000 visitors interested in each special exhibition
First and last week each attract 5% of interested visitors
Remaining visitors split evenly across other weeks
costs: Each exhibition incurs $3m fixed costs to stage (artwork acquisition/lease, expert curation, transport and installation)

exhibits.title: Annual Visitor Number Forecast for UK Museums (in millions)
exhibits.shows: Bar chart showing projected annual visitor numbers to all UK museums from 2022 to 2024, broken into three segments: UK Domestic Visitors, EU Visitors, and International Visitors (ex EU)

framework: Revenue: Identify breakdown of current commercial activity income (ticket sales, cafes & restaurants, in-gallery shop retail, publishing, venue hire, commercial filming, etc.); assess growth potential by revenue stream; evaluate pricing sensitivity; consider growing donations and corporate sponsorships

Costs: Determine what share of costs relate to commercial activities vs. public mission; break down commercial costs (special exhibition curation, permanent collection maintenance, marketing, labour, shops, cafes & restaurants); identify cost inefficiencies

Capabilities: Assess funding availability for proposed solutions; evaluate stakeholder buy-in (government, corporate sponsors, board members, key partners); determine whether current staff have sufficient skills or whether external expertise is needed

Risks: Evaluate whether profitability-oriented solutions are coherent with the National Gallery's brand image and public mission; assess whether solutions are short-term fixes or long-term sustainable; consider implementation and reputational risks

questions.prompt: The VP of Operations is evaluating reducing special exhibitions from 4 to 3 per year. Each exhibition currently lasts up to 11 weeks (with 2 weeks required between exhibitions to change display items). Using Exhibit 1, calculate profitability under each model and advise whether reducing to 3 exhibitions per year is a good idea.
questions.guidance: Candidates should calculate visitor numbers accounting for the capacity constraint, then compute revenue and costs for both models. A strong answer concludes that reducing to 3 exhibitions improves profitability because costs fall faster than revenue, but notes this conflicts with the National Gallery's public mission and may reduce overall visitor numbers and corporate sponsorship opportunities.

math.setup: Assume 50 weeks in a year. Current model: 4 exhibitions x 11 weeks = 44 weeks of exhibitions, plus 4 x 2 weeks changeover = 8 weeks; total = 52 weeks (the case uses 50 weeks as working assumption for new model calculation). New model: 3 exhibitions; each lasts (50 - 2x3)/3 = 44/3 ≈ 15 weeks. Interested visitors per exhibition = 500,000. First & last week = 5% each = 25,000 per week. Remaining interested = 450,000 spread across middle weeks. Max capacity = 40,000 per week.
steps: CURRENT MODEL (4 exhibitions, 11 weeks each): First & last week visitors: 500,000 x 0.05 = 25,000 per week; Middle weeks = 11 - 2 = 9 weeks; Middle weeks demand: (500,000 - 50,000) / 9 = 50,000 per week, but capped at 40,000; Visitors per exhibition: 25,000 x 2 + 40,000 x 9 = 50,000 + 360,000 = 410,000; Total visitors per year: 410,000 x 4 = 1,640,000; Revenue: 1,640,000 x $10 = $16.4m; Costs: $3m x 4 = $12m; Net profit: $16.4m - $12m = $4.4m

NEW MODEL (3 exhibitions, 15 weeks each): Each exhibition lasts (50 - 2x3)/3 = 15 weeks; First & last week: 25,000 each; Middle weeks = 13 weeks; Middle weeks demand: (500,000 - 50,000) / 13 = 34,615 per week, below 40,000 cap so no restriction; Visitors per exhibition: all 500,000 are admitted; Total visitors per year: 500,000 x 3 = 1,500,000; Revenue: 1,500,000 x $10 = $15m; Costs: $3m x 3 = $9m; Net profit: $15m - $9m = $6m
math.answer: Current model net profit = $4.4m/year; New model net profit = $6.0m/year. Reducing exhibitions to 3 per year improves profitability by $1.6m despite lower total revenue, because fixed costs decrease proportionally more than revenue.

questions.prompt: Although entry to permanent collection rooms is free, the National Gallery believes higher visitor numbers generate alternative revenue (donations, restaurant and shop purchases, higher prices for corporate events and filming). Exhibit 2 shows projected growth of visitor numbers for all UK museums for the next three years (post-Covid). What recommendation would you give to most effectively grow visitor numbers? What are the risks?
questions.guidance: Candidates should identify that the international visitors (ex EU) segment is growing fastest (from 22.5m to 35.9m over three years, roughly 60% growth), and therefore focus recommendations on strategies to attract international visitors. Risks around investment levels and reliability of international visitor numbers should be raised. An excellent answer also identifies other revenue-generating opportunities leveraging the National Gallery's international brand.

brainstorming.prompt: What strategies could the National Gallery use to attract more international visitors and leverage its international reputation to grow revenue?

categories.name: Attract more international visitors
ideas: Grow partnerships with tour operators serving international tourists
Employ assistants who speak international languages
Add more languages to audio guides
Grow international advertising to raise awareness of the Gallery

categories.name: Leverage international reputation for additional revenue
ideas: Lend permanent collection items to overseas museums
Generate consultant fees by helping less experienced museums in other countries curate exhibitions
Curate and deliver art courses in countries where the Gallery is well known
Set up a sister gallery in an overseas location

recommendation: The National Gallery can improve profitability through two main strategies: portfolio optimization and revenue growth

Portfolio optimization: reducing special exhibitions from 4 to 3 per year improves net profit from $4.4m to $6.0m because fixed costs drop faster than revenue; however this conflicts with the public mission

Revenue growth should focus on attracting international visitors (ex EU), the fastest-growing segment (projected 60%+ growth over 3 years), through partnerships with tour operators, multilingual services, and international advertising
risks: Reducing special exhibitions conflicts with the National Gallery's mission of welcoming the public and may reduce overall visitor numbers, impacting shop, cafe, and corporate sponsorship revenues
Attracting international visitors requires significant upfront investment and expertise in markets where the Gallery has limited existing knowledge
International visitor numbers are unreliable due to factors such as currency exchange rates, travel restrictions, and competition from other destinations
next_steps: Investigate feasibility of international visitor strategy by examining the National Gallery's available budget and current international market knowledge
Identify other revenue growth opportunities such as educational events, memberships, and merchandise
Evaluate stakeholder buy-in (government, board, corporate sponsors) for any reduction in exhibition frequency
